passage:
"Anand, isn't your solar system model due tomorrow?" asked Bhavna didi, looking up from her phone.
"Yes. It'll take ten minutes. I just need balls and paint."
"Do you have balls and paint?"
"Mummy has... something."
"Last time the volcano took you all Sunday."
"That was a volcano. This is just circles."
"Planets, a sun, sticks, labels..."
"It's easy, didi."
At 8 p.m. Anand was on the floor with newspaper and a half-painted Jupiter. At 9:30 the paint on Saturn still hadn't dried. At 10:15 he was crying because Mars had rolled under the sofa.
Bhavna crouched down beside him with a torch. "Ten minutes, na?" she said, and fished out Mars.

qa.q: What rolled under the sofa?
qa.a: Mars.

qa.q: Why was Anand so sure the model would take ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt confident and pictured only the easy path, forgetting that the volcano took all Sunday, so it seemed quick.

qa.q: What could Anand try for the next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the last one really took, list every part, and start a few days early.

qa.q: How does Bhavna didi seem to feel at 10:15?
qa.a: She seems amused but kind, teasing him gently while fishing out Mars with a torch.

grounding: A boy insists his model will take ten minutes, starts the night before and forgets how long his last project took.

passage: Last month our teacher gave us two weeks to write a book report. I thought, easy, it's only one page, I'll do it on the last night. I told Amandeep I'd finish in half an hour. Amandeep started reading the book on the first day. On the last night I opened the book and saw it had 160 pages. I had forgotten that I read slowly, and that the poem assignment took me three evenings. I read until eleven and only got to page 70. Papa found me asleep on the book. In the morning I wrote half a page about the first half. Now I think my brain shows me the fastest way it could go, not the way it usually goes. Deepak, 160 pages is not half an hour.

qa.q: How many pages did the book have?
qa.a: 160 pages.

qa.q: Why did Deepak think the report would take only half an hour?
qa.a: Deepak felt calm and confident, picturing the quickest way it could go and forgetting past slowness, like the poem that took three evenings.

qa.q: What could Deepak do with the next two-week assignment?
qa.a: Check how big the job is on the first day, remember how long similar work took, and do a little each day like Amandeep.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt the morning the report was due?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably relaxed and ready, having started reading on the first day.

grounding: A child recalls planning a book report for the last night, imagining the fastest path and forgetting past delays.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, science fair week
On Monday I asked each pair to estimate how long their diorama would take. Sahil said, "One evening, Miss. Easy." His partner Dolma said, "Maybe four evenings," and he laughed at her. When I reminded Sahil that his last project, the paper bridge, had taken him a week and still wasn't finished on the day, he said, "This one's different. It's smaller." The pair started on Thursday night. On Friday morning they arrived with a painted box, no animals and no labels. Sahil looked close to tears. Dolma had made the animals at home anyway, just in case, and they finished at lunch. I have asked every pair to write down how long their last project actually took before planning the next one.

qa.q: What did Dolma estimate?
qa.a: Maybe four evenings.

qa.q: Why did Sahil laugh at Dolma's estimate?
qa.a: He felt confident and sure it would be easy, imagining the quick version and ignoring how the paper bridge took a week.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new step helpful?
qa.a: Writing down how long the last project actually took makes children plan from real experience instead of the best-case picture.

qa.q: What might Dolma have felt on Friday morning?
qa.a: Dolma was probably relieved and a bit proud that her just-in-case animals saved the project.

grounding: A teacher records a boy who was sure a project would take one evening, ignoring his past delays, and ran out of time.

passage: On Friday evening in the kasba, Sarita pinned a chart above her bed: "SATURDAY: all of physics. SUNDAY: all of chemistry. Done!" Her elder sister Charu read it and raised an eyebrow. "Last term one chapter of optics took you four days." "That was different. I was lazy then. This weekend I'm focused." By Saturday noon Sarita was still on the second chapter of physics. The electricity went at four, and she worked by lantern until her eyes ached. On Sunday morning she looked at the untouched chemistry book and felt her stomach drop. "How is it only Sunday and I'm not even half done?" Charu brought her tea. "Want to make a real plan? Using how long chapters actually take you?" Sarita nodded, close to tears.

qa.q: How long did one chapter of optics take Sarita last term?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel on Sunday morning?
qa.a: She felt shocked and panicky, her stomach dropping, because the bright weekend plan was nowhere near done.

qa.q: What does Charu suggest, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Making a plan based on how long chapters actually take Sarita, rather than a hopeful picture of one focused weekend.

qa.q: How does Charu seem to see the chart?
qa.a: Charu doubts it from the start, remembering the four-day optics chapter, but comes with tea and help rather than blame.

grounding: A teenage girl plans to revise two whole subjects in a weekend, ignoring past experience, and is shocked when it takes far longer.

passage: On Friday afternoon in São Paulo, Clara and Priscila spread their history books across Clara's bedroom floor. "Twelve chapters, two days," Clara said, drawing a neat timetable. "Six a day. Easy. We'll have Sunday evening free for the park." Priscila reminded her that before the last test, a whole afternoon had gone on just two chapters. "That's because we kept watching videos," Clara said. "This time, pure focus." By Saturday night they had finished three chapters, and one of those only half. Clara's mum came in with sandwiches and found her staring at the timetable. "It looked so possible on Friday," Clara said. On Sunday there was no park. There was chapter five, and a new timetable, with only two chapters a day.

qa.q: How many chapters had they finished by Saturday night?
qa.a: Three chapters, and one of those only half.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling on Saturday night?
qa.a: Clara felt shocked and discouraged, staring at the timetable that had looked so possible on Friday.

qa.q: What change did the new timetable make, and why is it better?
qa.a: Two chapters a day, which matches how long chapters actually took them, instead of the hopeful six.

qa.q: How does Priscila's memory of the last test compare with Clara's plan?
qa.a: Priscila remembered two chapters taking a whole afternoon, a more realistic guide than Clara's six a day.

grounding: A teenager plans to revise a whole syllabus in one weekend, brushing aside past experience, and is shocked by how slowly it goes.

passage: In the girls' hostel study hall on Friday night, Simran taped a plan to her desk: "Saturday: botany. Sunday: zoology. Monday: rest!" Sabina, a senior, walked past and read it. "The whole syllabus?" "I've done it before," Simran said. She hadn't; last month two chapters of genetics had taken her a whole week. But that felt like a different, lazier Simran. By Saturday evening she was still on plant tissues, with thirteen chapters of botany left. She sat on the hostel steps, stunned. Sabina sat down beside her. "My first year, I made the same plan. It took me three weeks." She pulled out a notebook. "Write down how long each chapter really took you last time. Then we'll plan from that."

qa.q: How many chapters of botany were left on Saturday evening?
qa.a: Thirteen chapters.

qa.q: Why did Simran feel stunned on the hostel steps?
qa.a: She had pictured finishing botany in a day, so being stuck on plant tissues with thirteen chapters left came as a shock.

qa.q: What does Sabina suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Writing down how long each chapter really took last time and planning from that, so the timetable rests on experience rather than hope.

qa.q: What might Sabina feel seeing Simran's plan?
qa.a: Sabina probably felt sympathetic and a bit amused, remembering making the same plan herself in first year.

grounding: A teenage girl plans the whole syllabus for one weekend, ignoring how long past chapters took, and is stunned by her progress.

passage: When our hostel closed for renovation, I had to move into a shared flat across town. I told Sabina it would take one afternoon. I have one suitcase, I said, and some books. What I actually had, it turned out, was two years of stuff: a mattress, a table fan, three boxes of notes, a cycle and a cupboard full of things I'd forgotten. I didn't book a tempo until the day before, and all the tempos were taken, because every student was moving. At midnight before the handover I was carrying boxes down four floors, sweating and nearly in tears. Sabina's brother drove over with his van at 1 a.m. Now, whenever I'm sure something will take an afternoon, I ask myself how long the last move took. Farhan's rule.

qa.q: Who drove over with a van at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Sabina's brother.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling at midnight before the handover?
qa.a: Farhan felt panicked and exhausted, sweating and nearly in tears, because the one-afternoon move had become an all-night rush.

qa.q: What rule does Farhan follow now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking how long the last similar task took, so the plan starts from real experience rather than the best case.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt getting Farhan's call?
qa.a: Sabina was probably worried and sympathetic, asking her brother to help at 1 a.m.

grounding: A student recalls expecting a hostel move to take one afternoon and panicking at midnight before the deadline.

passage:
Supervisor's note, M.Sc. thesis meetings, 2 May
In January, Amandeep told me the thesis would take "six weeks, max": two weeks of experiments, two of analysis, two of writing. I asked how long the pilot experiment had taken last year; it had taken nine weeks. He said this time he knew the methods. Today, three weeks before submission, he came to my office pale. The experiments ran until April because the incubator failed twice, and he has not started writing. His lab mate Vikas, who planned from his own pilot timings and added extra weeks, submitted his draft yesterday. I sat with Amandeep and broke the writing into chapters, with a date for each. I have also asked the department about the extension process, in case it is needed.

qa.q: How long had the pilot experiment taken last year?
qa.a: Nine weeks.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep come to the office pale?
qa.a: He felt panicked and scared, with three weeks left and no writing started, after planning only for the six-week best case.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do to help, and what could Amandeep learn?
qa.a: Broke the writing into chapters with dates and checked on an extension; Amandeep could learn to plan from past timings as Vikas did.

qa.q: How did Vikas plan differently?
qa.a: Vikas planned from his own pilot timings and added extra weeks, so he submitted his draft early.

grounding: A supervisor records a student who planned a thesis on the best-case story and panicked near the deadline.

passage:
Thursday, 11:40 p.m.
The scholarship application closes at midnight tomorrow and I'm not even close. On Monday I told Chetan it was "one evening's work": a form and a short essay. Then today I found out it needs two recommendation letters, an attested income certificate and an essay of 800 words, not 300. Professor Iyer is out of town. The office that attests certificates shuts at five. Why do I always think things are a form and an essay? Last year's internship application had four hidden parts too.
Chetan came over at ten with chai and his own checklist from last year. We made a list: letters by email tonight, certificate first thing, essay by noon.
If I get through this, next time I open the form on day one.
Asif

qa.q: How many words must the essay be?
qa.a: 800 words, not 300.

qa.q: What is Asif feeling at 11:40 p.m.?
qa.a: Asif feels panicked and frustrated at not being close, having pictured one evening's work and forgotten last year's hidden parts.

qa.q: What did Chetan and Asif do, and what does Asif plan for next time?
qa.a: They made a list with a time for each part; next time Asif plans to open the form on day one.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel arriving with chai at ten?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels sympathetic and helpful, bringing a checklist from his own experience.

grounding: A student's diary shows underestimating a scholarship application and panicking the night before the deadline.

passage:
Team manager's note, design studio, 14 November
When our client Bhavna asked for a date for the new catalogue, Preeti didn't answer on the spot. She asked for an hour. In that hour she opened our project log and found the last three catalogues: they had taken five, seven and six weeks, although each was first promised in four. She broke the new job into parts: photography, layouts, two rounds of client changes, printing. She added a buffer of one week for the client changes, which have been late every time. Then she told Bhavna seven weeks. Bhavna was disappointed at first; another studio had said four. Today, in week six, the catalogue went to print. Bhavna called to say it was the first time a date had held. I will ask Preeti to show the team how she built the estimate.

qa.q: How long had the last three catalogues taken?
qa.a: Five, seven and six weeks.

qa.q: Why did Preeti ask for an hour instead of answering on the spot?
qa.a: She felt cautious about promising a hopeful date, knowing past catalogues ran late, so she wanted to check real figures first.

qa.q: What three things did Preeti do before promising a date?
qa.a: Checked how long similar catalogues took, broke the job into parts, and added a buffer for late client changes.

qa.q: How did Bhavna's feelings change from the first answer to week six?
qa.a: Bhavna was disappointed at first when another studio said four weeks, then pleased and relieved that a date finally held.

grounding: A manager records a young designer checking past project times, breaking the job into parts and adding a buffer before promising a date.

passage:
Tuesday
Nitin asked me today when the annual report would be ready. My mouth wanted to say "two weeks." It always wants to say two weeks. Instead I said, "Let me check and tell you tomorrow."
So tonight I opened my old calendar. Last year's report: started 3 Feb, finished 19 March. Six and a half weeks. The year before: seven. Both times I had promised two.
Broke it into pieces: data from four departments (always late, so a week), writing (two weeks), charts (a week), two rounds of edits (a week each, because Nitin always adds a section). That's six weeks, plus one for surprises.
Tomorrow I'll tell him seven weeks. He won't love it. But I'd rather disappoint him once on Wednesday than every Friday after.
Minakshi

qa.q: How long did last year's report take?
qa.a: Six and a half weeks, from 3 Feb to 19 March.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi hold back from saying two weeks?
qa.a: Minakshi felt wary of the old habit of promising two weeks and missing it, so checking real past timings felt safer.

qa.q: How did Minakshi build the seven-week estimate?
qa.a: By checking how long the last two reports took, breaking the job into parts with realistic times, and adding a week for surprises.

qa.q: How might Nitin react to hearing seven weeks?
qa.a: Nitin may be disappointed at first, but later relieved if the date holds instead of slipping every Friday.

grounding: A young worker's diary shows checking how long past reports took, breaking the job into parts and adding a buffer before promising a date.

passage: In the small Andheri office, the sprint board told the same story every month. Hafsa promised the reports module "by Friday," and it arrived the following Wednesday. Joel said "two days" and meant five. Santosh, the team lead, used to snap about it. This month he did something different. He put the last six months of estimates and actual dates on the big screen, everyone's, including his own. "Look," he said. "Every single one of us is late by about sixty percent. Me too. It's not laziness. It's how brains picture work." Hafsa laughed with relief. From then on, Santosh asked for two numbers: "If it goes well" and "If it goes like usual." He promised clients the second one. The board turned green for the first time in a year.

qa.q: By about how much was everyone late?
qa.a: About sixty percent.

qa.q: Why did Santosh put everyone's estimates on the screen, including his own?
qa.a: He had grown frustrated with snapping and felt curious about the real pattern, so he wanted everyone to see it was shared, not personal laziness.

qa.q: What two numbers did Santosh start asking for, and why?
qa.a: "If it goes well" and "if it goes like usual", so clients get the realistic date while hope still has a place.

qa.q: How did Hafsa react to the screen?
qa.a: She laughed with relief, seeing that everyone, even the lead, ran late in the same way.

grounding: A team lead sees repeated optimistic dates as a shared human pattern, reviews past accuracy and asks for two estimates.

passage:
"So, the survey analysis," Zainab said. "When?"
"Thursday," said Lavanya instantly.
"Okay. Can I show you something first? It's not a telling-off." Zainab turned her laptop round. "Your last five estimates, and when things actually landed."
Lavanya winced. "Oh no."
"Look closer. Everyone's are like this. Mine too. See, the office party budget: I said a day, it took four."
"So we're all just bad at this?"
"We're all human at this. Our brains picture the smooth version." Zainab smiled. "So give me two dates. One if nothing goes wrong. One if it goes the way yours usually go."
Lavanya thought. "Thursday if the data's clean. Next Tuesday if it's like the last three times."
"Then I'll tell the client Tuesday, and we'll both be happy if it's Thursday."

qa.q: How long did Zainab's office party budget take?
qa.a: Four days, though Zainab had said a day.

qa.q: Why did Zainab say it wasn't a telling-off?
qa.a: Zainab saw the late dates as a shared human pattern, not laziness, and wanted Lavanya to feel safe rather than blamed.

qa.q: Why is asking for two dates helpful?
qa.a: It keeps the hopeful estimate but gives the client the realistic one, based on how Lavanya's tasks usually go.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she saw her estimates?
qa.a: She winced at first, embarrassed, then felt better seeing that everyone's were the same.

grounding: A team lead shows a colleague past estimates next to real dates, treats the gap as human thinking and asks for a range.

passage: In my first year as team lead, I thought Ojas was just slack. Every estimate he gave me was cheerful and wrong: "two days," then five; "this week," then next. I started to feel irritated whenever he spoke in stand-up. Then one Sunday I went through my own old diary from when I was a developer. My estimates were exactly the same, cheerful and wrong. I hadn't been lazy then. I'd just pictured the easy path every time. So on Monday I didn't lecture Ojas. I made a small sheet for the whole team: your guess, the real time, and a column for what happened. After two months we could all see our average slip. Now we plan with it. Ojas told me later, "Shankar, I thought you hated me in March." I didn't. I just hadn't recognised myself.

qa.q: What columns did the team's sheet have?
qa.a: Your guess, the real time, and what happened.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling toward Ojas at first?
qa.a: Shankar felt irritated, thinking Ojas was slack, before recognising the same cheerful mistakes in the old diary.

qa.q: Why did the sheet work better than a lecture?
qa.a: It showed the whole team their own average slip, turning a blame problem into a shared pattern they could plan with.

qa.q: How had Ojas felt in March?
qa.a: Ojas thought Shankar hated him, so he probably felt anxious and judged.

grounding: A young lead recalls seeing a teammate's optimistic dates as a human pattern after recognising the same in their own past estimates.

passage:
Monday. Saurabh watched a video about three famous creators who had dropped out of school at sixteen and "never looked back." By bedtime he had told his mother he wanted to quit after Class 10 and make videos full-time. "They did it. It's easy if you're serious."
Wednesday. His aunt Sangeeta, who worked at a media company, came for dinner. "How many kids do you think tried the same thing that year?" she asked. Saurabh shrugged. "Those three made it." "We get two hundred applications a month from young creators," she said. "Most have under a hundred followers after two years. You never see them, because nobody makes videos about them."
Saturday. Saurabh looked up the channels of people who had started when those three did. Most had stopped posting. He didn't delete his camera app. But he did pick up his Class 10 timetable again.

qa.q: How many applications a month does Sangeeta's company get from young creators?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did quitting school seem easy to Saurabh on Monday?
qa.a: He felt inspired and excited by three success stories, never seeing the many who tried and quietly failed.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do on Saturday, and why was it useful?
qa.a: He looked up others who started at the same time and saw most had stopped, which showed him the missing failures.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's mother have felt on Monday night?
qa.a: She was probably worried and alarmed to hear him plan to quit after Class 10 because of one video.

grounding: Over a week, a teenage boy decides dropping out is easy after seeing three success stories, until he looks for those who failed.

passage: Kunal, you say the cricketers on TV skipped studies and did fine, so you can too? Let your Wasim uncle tell you about my own sixteenth year. Our town had one boy, Irshad, who had played for the state team. Everyone talked about him. He had left school after Class 9. So I decided the same path would work for me. I skipped exams to practise at the maidan every day. What I didn't see were the thirty other boys at that maidan who had made the same choice over the years. They weren't on TV. They were driving autos, working in shops, some still bitter. I only found out when our coach, old Hameed sir, sat me down and named them one by one. That evening I went to my teacher and asked for the missed papers.

qa.q: After which class did Irshad leave school?
qa.a: After Class 9.

qa.q: Why did young Wasim believe skipping exams would work?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and inspired by Irshad, the only one everyone talked about, and never saw the boys for whom it didn't work.

qa.q: What turning point changed Wasim's path?
qa.a: Hameed sir naming the thirty other boys one by one, after which Wasim asked his teacher for the missed papers.

qa.q: Why might Hameed sir have named the boys one by one?
qa.a: He probably cared about Wasim and knew that real, familiar faces would make the missing failures impossible to ignore.

grounding: An uncle recalls believing, at sixteen, that skipping school for cricket was a sure path because he only saw the one who made it.

passage: The stream-change form was due at 9 a.m., and at 10 p.m. the power went out across the colony. By phone light, Himani showed Thomas the magazine: "Ten founders under thirty who left school early." "See? They skipped all this and built companies. I'm dropping science tomorrow." Thomas, her classmate from the flat below, scrolled on his own phone in the dark. "Okay, but how many people left school to start a company and didn't make a magazine?" "Nobody knows that." "Exactly. Nobody writes that list." He found an article about the hundreds of start-ups that close in their first year. Himani read it by the flickering screen. At 8:40 the next morning she was still in the science stream, with a new notebook titled "Company ideas, weekends only."

qa.q: When was the stream-change form due?
qa.a: At 9 a.m.

qa.q: Why did dropping science feel like a good idea to Himani?
qa.a: She felt excited and inspired by ten founders who left school, not seeing the many who tried and never made a magazine.

qa.q: What did Thomas's question do for Himani?
qa.a: Asking how many didn't make the magazine pointed her to the missing failures, so she kept science and planned her ideas for weekends.

qa.q: What was it like for Thomas to argue by phone light?
qa.a: Thomas seemed calm and caring, gently pointing her to the missing list instead of mocking her idea.

grounding: Under a deadline, a teenage girl nearly drops a subject after reading about founders who left school, until a friend asks about those who failed.

passage: Hafsa's alarm went off at 4 a.m. in the Koramangala flat for the ninth day in a row. She had read that three famous founders all woke at four, drank black coffee and never checked messages before noon. So she did the same, yawning through her 9 a.m. lecture and snapping at Ojas, her flatmate, when he played music. "This is how successful people live," she said. Ojas looked up from his laptop. "How many people wake at four and don't build a company?" "I don't know." "Millions, probably. Bakers. Security guards. My uncle, who is tired and broke." Hafsa laughed, then stopped. "So the four o'clock thing isn't why they succeeded?" "Maybe. Maybe not. You only see the ones who got famous."

qa.q: What time did Hafsa's alarm go off?
qa.a: At 4 a.m.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa believe waking at four would make her successful?
qa.a: She felt inspired and hopeful after reading about three famous founders, never thinking of all the people with the same habit who never became famous.

qa.q: What could Hafsa check before copying a founder's habit?
qa.a: Whether people without success share the same habit, and whether it actually suits her own sleep and lectures.

qa.q: How does Ojas see the four o'clock routine?
qa.a: Ojas sees it as a habit shared by millions, most of them not famous, so he doubts it explains success.

grounding: A student copies famous founders' early-rising habits without noticing how many people share the habit without success.

passage:
"I'm leaving the MBA after first year," Tanuja announced at dinner. "All the big founders dropped out."
Uday put down his roti. "All?"
"Well. The famous ones. There's a list."
"Who made the list?"
"A magazine."
"Did the magazine list the people who dropped out and failed?"
"...Why would they?"
"Exactly. It's a list of winners. If a thousand people drop out and five succeed, you only hear about the five."
"You don't know it's a thousand."
"You don't know it's five. That's my point." Uday pushed the dal towards her. "Find ten people who left and didn't make it. Then decide."
Tanuja stabbed a potato. "Fine. I'll look." She paused. "Where do you even find people who failed?"
"Ask the college alumni office. They know who left."

qa.q: Where does Uday suggest finding people who left?
qa.a: The college alumni office.

qa.q: Why is Tanuja so sure leaving the MBA is a good idea?
qa.a: She feels excited and certain because the famous founders on the magazine list dropped out, without seeing the many who dropped out and failed.

qa.q: What does Uday suggest before deciding, and why?
qa.a: Finding ten people who left and didn't make it, so she sees the whole group, not only the winners.

qa.q: How does Uday see the magazine list?
qa.a: Uday sees it as a list of winners only, which hides everyone who dropped out and failed.

grounding: A student plans to copy famous founders by dropping out, and a family member points out the list shows only the winners.

passage: In second year, I became obsessed with how famous founders worked. I read that the best known ones slept four hours, skipped classes to build things, and never made plans, just "moved fast." So I did all three. I skipped lectures to work on an app idea, slept at 3 a.m., and called my messy weeks "moving fast." My marks fell and the app never launched. My friend Zeenat, who was studying economics, asked me one day, "Lalit, how many students did exactly what you're doing and failed?" I said there was no way to know. She said, "That's the point. The ones who failed don't give interviews." I still like building things. But now I look at what worked for many people, not only what worked for the famous few.

qa.q: What was Zeenat studying?
qa.a: Economics.

qa.q: Why did Lalit copy the founders' habits?
qa.a: Lalit felt inspired and excited by the famous stories, believing the habits were the reason for their success.

qa.q: What does Lalit look at now, and why is it better?
qa.a: What worked for many people, not just the famous few, because the failures with the same habits don't give interviews.

qa.q: How did Zeenat seem to see Lalit's plan?
qa.a: Zeenat seemed doubtful but caring, asking a question that pointed to all the students who tried the same and failed.

grounding: A student recalls copying famous founders' habits without seeing the many with the same habits who failed.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
Thanks for sending the brochure for the data-science bootcamp. I can see why you're excited: those six alumni stories are impressive, and one of them now works at a big firm.
Before we recommend it to our juniors, though, I'd like to ask the bootcamp a few questions. How many people started in each batch? How many finished? Of those, how many found jobs in data within a year? The brochure shows six faces, but it doesn't say whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.
If the numbers look good, I'll happily be the first to sign our juniors up. If they won't share them, that tells us something too.
Shall I write to them tomorrow?
Ishita

qa.q: How many alumni stories does the brochure show?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why does Ishita want to ask questions before recommending the bootcamp?
qa.a: Ishita feels cautious, because six impressive faces don't show whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.

qa.q: Which questions does Ishita want answered, and why do they matter?
qa.a: How many started, finished and found data jobs within a year, because only the whole batch shows whether the course really works.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading the email?
qa.a: Farhan might feel slightly deflated but respected, since the excitement is acknowledged and a fair next step is offered.

grounding: A young professional asks for the whole batch's results before praising a course that advertises only its success stories.

passage: Tenzin, people ask why Seema, the agriculture officer, didn't just push the new mulching method everywhere after the success stories. Here's why. The company brought us five farmers who had doubled their yields. Five beautiful fields, great photos. The officers around me were ready to print posters. But I asked, "How many farmers tried it in total?" Silence. Then someone admitted it was sixty-two. So I asked to see the other fifty-seven. Some had average results. Many had lost crops, because the method needs water they didn't have. The five were all near the canal. If I had looked only at the winners, I'd have sent the method to dry villages and ruined a season. Now I always ask the same thing first: who's missing from this picture?

qa.q: How many farmers had tried the method in total?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when the other officers wanted to print posters?
qa.a: Seema felt cautious and a little uneasy, sensing that five photos couldn't show the whole picture.

qa.q: What question did Seema ask, and what did it reveal?
qa.a: How many farmers tried it in total; it revealed fifty-seven others, many of whom lost crops without canal water.

qa.q: What would change for farmers in dry villages if Seema had not asked?
qa.a: They might have been pushed into a method that needs water they didn't have, and lost a season's crops.

grounding: A young officer asks how many farmers tried a method and what happened to the rest before praising it.

passage: I'm Pema, and I teach in the room next to Jasleen's, so I was at the staff meeting when the principal held up the results. "The five students who used the new revision app all scored above ninety. We should make it compulsory." Everyone nodded. Jasleen raised her hand. "Ma'am, how many students used the app in total?" The principal checked. Forty. "And the other thirty-five?" Nobody knew. Jasleen offered to find out. Over the next week I saw her in the staff room every lunch with the class registers, adding columns. The other thirty-five had scored just like everyone else. The five toppers had always been toppers. At the next meeting, the principal thanked her and said the app would stay optional. I can't say what Jasleen felt, but she was smiling as she packed up the registers.

qa.q: How many students had used the app in total?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What might Jasleen's smile suggest?
qa.a: She probably felt satisfied and relieved that the full picture was seen before the app was made compulsory.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do before accepting the praise for the app?
qa.a: She asked how many used it in total and what happened to the other thirty-five, then checked the registers.

qa.q: How did the principal react to Jasleen's findings?
qa.a: The principal thanked her and kept the app optional instead of compulsory.

grounding: A colleague describes a young teacher asking about the students missing from a success story before a method is praised.

passage: The site visit was running late, it was forty-two degrees, and the old contractor would not stop talking. "Look at that haveli across the street," he told Sangeeta ma'am, the senior architect. "Two hundred years and not one crack. Today's buildings fall down in twenty." Jagdish, the trainee, wiped his forehead and looked along the street. The haveli stood beautifully. But on either side were empty plots and one pile of old bricks where, the chaiwala said, houses from the same time had collapsed or been pulled down long ago. "Sir," Jagdish said, "maybe we only see the old ones that were strong. The weak ones aren't here any more." The contractor frowned. Sangeeta ma'am smiled for the first time that afternoon. "Write that down," she said. "We'll put it in the report."

qa.q: What was on either side of the haveli?
qa.a: Empty plots and one pile of old bricks.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he looked along the street?
qa.a: Jagdish was hot and tired but curious, noticing the empty plots and wondering what had happened to the other old houses.

qa.q: What did Jagdish point out, and why is it a fair correction?
qa.a: That only the strong old buildings still stand because the weak ones collapsed or were removed, so the survivors make old building look better than it was.

qa.q: How did the contractor react to Jagdish's point?
qa.a: The contractor frowned, probably not pleased to have his story questioned.

grounding: On a hot, rushed site visit, a young trainee notices that only the durable old buildings remain to be admired.

passage: At the family dinner in their Delhi flat, the radio played an old film song, and Pooja masi sighed. "They don't make music like this any more. Every song from our time was a gem. Today it's all noise." Varun, twenty-four, smiled and pulled up a list on his phone: every film song released in 1975. There were hundreds. He read a few titles aloud. Nobody at the table recognised them. "Masi, these are from your time too," he said. "We only hear the ones that were so good people kept playing them for fifty years. The rest disappeared." Pooja masi laughed and swatted his arm. "So you're saying my generation also made noise?" "Some. Just like mine. In fifty years, only our best will be left."

qa.q: Which year's film songs did Varun look up?
What does Varun's smile suggest as he pulls up the list?
qa.a: He felt amused and curious rather than annoyed, wanting to show Pooja masi the full picture gently.

qa.q: What point does Varun make, and why is it fair?
qa.a: That only the best old songs are still played while the forgotten ones vanished, so the old era sounds better than it was.

qa.q: How does Pooja masi take Varun's point?
qa.a: She laughs and swats his arm, taking it in good humour.

grounding: A young man hears that old songs were all better and points out that only the lasting ones are still heard.

passage:
"Look at this," said Arohi, holding up an old steel tiffin at the office lunch table. "My Nani's. Fifty years old. Things were made properly back then. My new one broke in six months."
Lalremsiami tapped it. "It's lovely. But how many tiffins did your Nani's family buy in those fifty years?"
"I don't know. A few?"
"And where are the rest?"
Arohi paused. "Thrown away, I suppose. Or broken."
"So we see this one because it's the strongest. The weak ones from that time are gone."
"You're saying old things weren't better made?"
"Some were. But we only get to see the survivors."
Arohi turned the tiffin over, looking at the dents. "Nani did say she lost two on a train once."
"See? Even the good ones had bad luck."

qa.q: How long did Arohi's new tiffin last?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami seem to feel about Arohi's claim?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seems curious and friendly rather than dismissive, praising the tiffin before asking where the others went.

qa.q: What question helps Arohi see the full picture?
qa.a: Where are the rest of the tiffins from that time? It shows that only the strongest one survived to be seen.

qa.q: How does Arohi's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: Arohi moves from sure that old things were better made to remembering Nani lost two, seeing that only survivors remain.

grounding: A young professional hears that old things were better made and notes that only the durable ones are still around.

passage: That month at Deepak's school, everyone at recess had spinning battle tops, the plastic kind that crashed together in a bowl. Deepak had always spent recess drawing comics under the neem tree with Jasleen. Now he begged his father every night for a top. "Everyone has one. EVERYONE." When he finally got one, he stood at the edge of the circle, crashing it half-heartedly, and lost every round. "Do you even like it?" Jasleen asked at the water tap. "Of course," he said quickly. "It's the best game." But at home that evening he took out his comic notebook and drew for an hour without stopping, and hid the top under his bed.

qa.q: Where did Deepak and Jasleen used to draw comics?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Deepak beg for a top he didn't really enjoy?
qa.a: He felt left out and wanted to belong, so having what everyone had mattered more than whether he liked it.

qa.q: How could Deepak's father or teacher help?
qa.a: Notice how much Deepak loves drawing and help him find friends who enjoy comics too, so he can belong without pretending.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel when Deepak stops drawing with her?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel lonely and a bit hurt, missing their comics under the neem tree.

grounding: A boy begs for the toy everyone has and pretends to love it, though he would rather be drawing.

passage:
Monday. Manoj went to school with his green dinosaur bag, the one he had chosen himself. By lunch he noticed that every boy in Class 3 had the same blue superhero bag. "Dinosaurs are for babies," one of them said.
Wednesday. Manoj asked his mother for the blue bag. "But you love dinosaurs," she said. "Not any more," he said, not looking at her. His sister Preeti heard him tell a friend on the phone that he now "hated" dinosaurs.
Saturday. The new blue bag came. Manoj wore it proudly on the stairs. That evening, though, Preeti found him in his room with the old green bag in his lap, running his finger over the stegosaurus. "You can keep both," she whispered. He nodded, and tucked the dinosaur bag into his cupboard, carefully, where he could see it.

qa.q: What bag did every boy in Class 3 have?
qa.a: The same blue superhero bag.

qa.q: Why did Manoj say he hated dinosaurs?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of being left out after the babies comment, so he changed his taste to match the group.

qa.q: What could help Manoj keep what he loves while fitting in?
qa.a: Knowing he can keep both, as Preeti said, and perhaps finding a friend who also likes dinosaurs.

qa.q: What was it like for Preeti to find Manoj with the old bag?
qa.a: Preeti was probably touched and a bit sad to see he still loved the dinosaur bag, and wanted to comfort him.

grounding: Over a week, a boy gives up his dinosaur bag for the one every classmate has, though he still loves the old one.

passage: Omkar, you want the same card game everyone has, even though you love puzzles? Let your Jyoti dadi tell you about your Dadaji when he was nine. In our town that year, every boy had a kite with sharp string for the fights on the rooftops. Your Dadaji hated kite fights; his fingers got cut, and he was scared of the roof's edge. What he loved was fixing old clocks. But he begged his father for a kite, cried for three days, and got one. He stood on the roof every evening losing every fight, fingers cut, pretending he loved it. Then one day his friend Babloo came down and found him fixing a broken clock in the shop instead. Babloo sat and watched for an hour. After that the two of them fixed clocks together, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did young Dadaji love doing?
qa.a: Fixing old clocks.

qa.q: Why did young Dadaji beg for a kite he didn't enjoy?
qa.a: He wanted to belong and was afraid of being left out, so having what every boy had mattered more than his own love of clocks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Babloo came down and watched him fix a clock; sharing what he truly loved gave him a friend and belonging without pretending.

qa.q: What might Babloo have felt sitting and watching for an hour?
qa.a: Babloo was probably curious and fascinated, discovering something new with his friend.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a boy who begged for the kite every boy had and pretended to love it, though he loved fixing clocks.
